evidence_quotes.quote: Chaque cas d’étude met en évidence un mode d’hybridation différent entre systèmes traditionnels et systèmes modernes de l’eau.

L’intervention croissante de l’État fut consolidée en 1963 par les lois de « Nationalisation de l’eau » et de « Préservation et revitalisation des eaux souterraines », puis mise en œuvre après la création du Ministère de l’Eau et de l’Énergie en 1964, instituant l’État comme gestionnaire des eaux et de l’électricité (Aghâh, Hassani Saadi, 2015).
ils sont aujourd’hui connectés au système d’adduction moderne de la ville et rechargés en hiver. Les résidents de chaque quartier en bénéficient pour leur consommation courante en été.
Le recours aux puits profonds, aux barrages et aux transferts interbassins a eu des conséquences négatives sur l’accès à l’eau
The article takes stock of this extremely rapid transition from a traditional and ancestral system, inherited from the water-led civilization of Persia, towards a universal model of water supply.

criterion_notes.c1: Although the paper primarily examines historical and contemporary urban morphology (integration between hydraulic networks and urban spatial structures) and basin-scale water resources, its three urban case studies (Semnan, Naeen, Tehran) include community/municipal potable water supply systems and neighborhood water access in residential quarters.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading: the paper examines physical hydraulic infrastructure modernization (large dams, deep pumped wells, modern urban road/planning grids, and inter-basin water transfers replacing traditional qanats and bands) and macro-governance background, rather than any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community service access (no analysis of eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs/cost-recovery, discretion, disconnection/enforcement, or utility regulatory structure governing household access; a brief mention of Semnan private water-right holders retaining river shares concerns irrigation of historic orchards and gardens). Under the plain/literal broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper arguably touches on institutional/governance factors (1963/1967 water nationalization laws, creation of the Ministry of Water and Energy in 1964, and centralized state management versus traditional decentralized private/waqf/communal water-sharing), so it passes plain C2 in isolation as macro-governance discussion, though governance remains unanalysed macro-historical background and the overall plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude due to lack of an identifiable empirical design linking governance to household/community service-access outcomes (c5) and non-core scope under Criterion 10.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains three comparative urban-hydraulic case studies (Tehran, Semnan, Naeen) using cartographic/morphological analysis of historical maps, 1956 aerial photography, and 2020 satellite imagery alongside secondary hydrological/municipal statistics and field inquiry conducted between 2015 and 2019, though fieldwork and interview methods are not formally reported.
criterion_notes.c4: Alongside urban morphological integration, aquifer depletion, and river drying, the paper descriptively reports municipal supply source shares (e.g., 75% of Semnan inhabitants using the modern potable network vs. 25% using traditional reservoirs in 1975) and seasonal service continuity/shortages in Naeen (regular summer potable-water shutoffs mitigated since 2016 by winter recharge of 46 neighborhood reservoirs supplying 23,000 m3 to residential quarters).
criterion_notes.c5: No formal methods section is provided for the 2015-2019 fieldwork or hydraulic-engineer interviews, there is no household or community sample, and the paper does not specify an identifiable empirical study design isolating a governance exposure against household or community water service-access outcomes (access figures are sporadic secondary citations embedded in a macro-historical urban-morphology narrative).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in French with an English abstract (PDF Page 28 of 28). Direct reading/translation from French is feasible per Criterion 10, so language does not prevent assessment, though as an out-of-scope urban-morphology and macro water-resources paper it is not potentially important for review inclusion.

study_design: Historical-geographical and urban-morphological comparative case study (three cities, using historical/aerial cartography, secondary reports, and unspecified 2015-2019 fieldwork)
population_and_sample: Three Iranian cities examined as urban-hydraulic territorial systems — Tehran, Semnân, and Nâeen — plus the Zayandeh-Rud river basin (unit of analysis: city / urban-hydraulic system / river basin; no household sample)
exposure: Hydraulic and urban modernization since the 1920s (transition from traditional qanats, bands, and neighborhood reservoirs to large dams, deep pumped wells, modern urban planning grids, inter-basin water transfers, and centralized state water management)
outcome: Socio-spatial integration of hydraulic infrastructure and urban form, municipal/basin water withdrawal volumes, aquifer depletion, and descriptive municipal supply shares and summer potable-water cutoffs in residential neighborhoods
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While the paper's three Iranian urban case studies (Semnân, Nâeen, Tehran) touch on municipal potable water supply and summer drinking-water cutoffs in residential neighborhoods, its core focus is the historical and morphological integration of physical hydraulic infrastructures (qanâts, bands, reservoirs vs. large dams, deep wells, and inter-basin transfers) with urban spatial structures and basin-level water-resource sustainability. Under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, it does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community service access; state water nationalization (1963/1967) and centralization appear only as macro-historical background. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper would be excluded because fieldwork methods (2015-2019) are unreported and no empirical study design linking a governance exposure to household/community service-access outcomes is identifiable (c5 = no).
